title: Deuxième partie : variations sur l'équation des lacets [suite à La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois…, pages 293 à 650, dont table des matières] : notes et copies de notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting, continued from the previous pages. pi is a group and rho is an automorphism of pi of finite order n. Write pi~ = pi ⋊ <rho> for the semidirect product, which is the extension (3) of Z/n by pi. A splitting of (3) is given by an element rho'_g = g·rho with g in pi and (g rho)^n = 1. Equivalently g·rho(g)···rho^{n-1}(g) = 1; this is equation (8), the 'loop equation'. So the solutions of (8) are exactly the nonabelian 1-cocycles Z^1(Z/n, pi). Conjugation by alpha acts on splittings by g ↦ alpha g rho(alpha)^{-1}, which is twisted conjugation (formula (14)). Its orbits under pi are the classes in H^1(Z/n, pi).

This page checks that enlarging the acting group from pi to pi~ gives nothing new.
- Write alpha in pi~ as alpha = alpha_0 rho^i, with alpha_0 in pi and i in Z.
- Then alpha·rho(alpha)^{-1} = alpha_0·rho(alpha_0)^{-1}, which is (19). So the 'trivial' cocycles coming from pi~ are already coboundaries coming from pi.
- More generally, alpha g rho(alpha)^{-1} = alpha_0 rho^i(g) rho(alpha_0)^{-1}.
- Moreover rho^i(g) is itself pi-twisted-conjugate to g: rho^i(g) = beta g rho(beta)^{-1} with beta = (g rho(g)···rho^{i-1}(g))^{-1}. Check: beta g rho(beta)^{-1} = (g···rho^{i-1}g)^{-1}·g·(rho g···rho^i g) = rho^i(g).
- Hence alpha·g = (alpha_0 beta)·g, so pi~-orbits on Z^1 coincide with pi-orbits.

Grothendieck then remarks that the parametrisation (18) of coboundaries alpha·rho(alpha)^{-1} is no longer injective modulo pi once alpha ranges over pi~. For example, alpha = rho gives g = 1.

He next generalises to a larger group E ⊃ pi~ in which pi is normal, so that 1 → pi → E → G → 1. The model case is pi = pi_{0,3} (the free profinite or discrete group of P^1 minus 3 points), with E = S_{0,3}, the extension of S_3 by pi_{0,3}, and pi~ the inverse image of the cyclic group {1, rho, rho^2}. The next page shows that the subgroup E_rho of elements whose image in G centralises rho acts on the cocycles. That action can permute the H^1 classes nontrivially.

Purpose: to study the set of solutions of the 'loop equation', i.e. the order-3 (or order-n) relation of hexagon/Grothendieck–Teichmüller type, modulo conjugation, and the symmetries acting on it.
errors: The formula beta = (g rho(g)···rho^{i-1}(g))^{-1} only makes sense for i ≥ 0, which is why (19) is stated for i in N, whereas just above i ranges over Z. This is harmless: since rho^n = 1, one may reduce i mod n to 0 ≤ i < n. It is a small inconsistency, not an error.

ideas.what: Solutions of g rho(g)···rho^{n-1}(g) = 1 as splittings of pi ⋊ Z/n, modulo twisted conjugation
ideas.modern_name: Nonabelian cohomology H^1(Z/n, pi); conjugacy classes of complements / torsion elements in a semidirect product
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard (Serre, Cohomologie galoisienne; classical group theory)
ideas.where_published: Related material in La Longue Marche (1981) and Esquisse d'un programme; not this exact computation as far as known

ideas.what: The action of pi~ = pi ⋊ <rho> on cocycles reduces to the pi-action, via rho^i(g) = beta g rho(beta)^{-1}
ideas.modern_name: Inner action of the acting group on H^1 is trivial (the 'rho acts trivially on H^1(<rho>, pi)' lemma)

ideas.what: Action of the normaliser/centraliser-preimage E_rho of a larger extension E (e.g. S_{0,3} ⊃ pi_{0,3}) on the solution set
ideas.modern_name: Outer action on H^1; the setting of the hexagon equation in Grothendieck–Teichmüller theory
ideas.usually_credited_to: Drinfeld (1990), Ihara; Grothendieck (Esquisse) for the general programme

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful but routine nonabelian-cohomology verification: the inner action is trivial on H^1 of a cyclic group. It is preparatory material for the loop equation in the pi_{0,3} / S_{0,3} setting. Nothing here is new to a specialist.
transcription_corrections: Use consistent notation: the image writes lowercase pi and pi~ throughout this page, while the previous-page transcription uses Pi.
In (19), the image clearly reads 'pour alpha = alpha_0 rho^i, i ∈ N' (natural numbers), as transcribed.
The last line likely reads 'dans lequel pi soit [invariant / extension]…'. The phrase 'a une extension invariant' is garbled; the sense is that pi is a normal subgroup of E.
